subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF DOMINION GOVERNMENT IN RELATION TO THE ENTERPRISE
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are
proceeded with I think it fitting that I should make some reference to the Beauharnois undertaking in view of statements made a few days ago which I have since 'had an opportunity to look through. I shall be as brief as possible, but I desire to correct some misapprehensions that are apparently in the minds of hon. gentlemen diagonally opposite and opposite and to my right. I think nothing better illustrates the soundness of the old maxim that it is very unwise to endeavour to lock the stable after the horse has been stolen, or the truth that is embodied in the couplet with which most of the house is familiar:
Not heaven itself upon the past hath power: What has been has been.	.
Nothing better illustrates the truth of these statements than the position of Beauharnois, and when hon. gentlemen suggest, as they did in this house, that the federal government of the country should engage in the power business and should expropriate the power enterprise at Beauharnois, they overlooked two essential facts. The first is that the province of Quebec leased the power, not -the Dominion government; and it leased the power believing that it had the legal right so to do. The ex-Minister of Justice referred to the fact that a similar attitude of mind was expressed by the government of Ontario in connection with the power development carried on at Niagara and other points on the St. Lawrence river. The second point to which I direct attention is that contracts were made between Beauharnois undertaking and two customers, namely, the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario and the Montreal Light, Heat -and Power Company, which contracts are outstanding and are valid contracts according to the law of the country in which they were made.
If this house will bear in mind these two facts it will at once realize and recognize the extent to which this government was unable to deal with the problems to which attention has been directed. Reference has -been made to the fact that on more than one occasion I have directed attention to the circumstances connected with the alienation of natural resources by the governments of this country. What the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) overlooked, in quoting again the statement I made originally, was that the 53719-324
crown is not the crown in right of the dominion only but is also the -crown in right of each of the provinces. Only last year the privy council, in a very important case, decided that while the crown was one and indivisible, nevertheless there was a crown in right of the provinces and a crown in right of the dominion.
If it will Ibe borne in mind that the power rights with respect to the St. Lawrence are claimed by the crown in right of the province of Quebec and not by the crown in right of the dominion, so far as this particular case is concerned, my observations with respect to the regret that the government must experience because the crown has parted with its rights will have full force and effect. Bear in mind, therefore, that as a result of the investigation! in this house, the government took the only appropriate action which it could take under its constitutional limitations. It declared certain works to be for the benefit of Canada, it rescinded and repealed an order in council under which certain claims were made and it passed a statute by which no further alienations, so far as the government was concerned, of its rights in the St. Lawrence river to give additional water to the enterprise, would be valid without the consent, not of the executive but of this parliament.
I shall not traverse the ground which has been covered with respect to these contracts and to the legislation enacted by this parliament after the report was made by the investigating committee. I shall content myself with referring to the statements which were made in the house in 1932 as to what we conceived -our duty to be with respect to the enterprise itself. Before I do that perhaps I should direct attention to the fact that the contract with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, to which I referred, contained a provision by which the Beauharnois company undertook not to compete with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated in the distribution of power on the island of Montreal or within the radius of so many miles from the Place d'Armes square. So far as distribution of power was concerned, the company had contracted itself out of the right to sell power in that particular area which is the -most populous and the largest power consuming area in a particular community in the country.
I said that the purpose of the government as declared i-n this house was fourfold, and I shall quote from a statement which I made in this house in 1932, as follows:
The government by every means in its power will endeavour to do the following: (a) secure

Beauharnois-Mr. Bennett

continuance of the enterprise; (b) secure the rights of those who bona fide have put their money in that enterprise; (c) secure proper control and management; (d) take such other steps as may be necessary when terms and conditions are fixed as will ensure the greatest possible benefit to this dominion as a whole by reason of the undertaking now being declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.
Those were the four ends the government had in view. First, as to the continuance of the enterprise, it was found that the $30,000,000 which had been given to the company by investors throughout Canada was not sufficient to enable the company to continue its operations and, further, that the company could not secure additional money by making sale of its first mortgage bonds. Therefore, the government undertook to be responsible for any ultimate loss that might be made by the bankers in the advances which were given to the enterprise, on the condition that the enterprise should convey the canal itself to the crown in the right of the dominion so that if the St. Lawrence seaway undertaking was carried out this would be part of and available for the purposes of the seaway. The cost was represented by something in the neighbourhood of the sum which the government ultimately became responsible for in the event of the banks not realizing on their security, namely, between $15,000,000 and $16,000,000. In pursuance of that undertaking the enterprise was carried forward so that on the first day of October last power was delivered to the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario and the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, thereby making possible the continuance of the corporation as such. Had the work not been placed in operation by the first day of October, the contracts would have fallen and in these days I am not sure but that both the hydro and the Montreal Light, Heat and Power would have been glad if the power had not been made available. The power was made available on the first day of October through the efforts taken by the administration. ,
Attention was directed to the fact that shortly after the house rose when we first had to deal with this matter the Premier of Quebec suggested that we should turn over the undertaking to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated and relieve ourselves from any further responsibility in the premises. I said then that although the undertaking had been launched for the purpose of being a competitor of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, I could quite understand the attitude of the Premier of Quebec who did not believe that government should be in-

volved in matters of this kind. Nevertheless I represented that we could not agree to do this for the simple reason that that great corporation was not interested in seeing this corporation succeed, having regard to the then existing conditions. In view of what had transpired in this parliament, we felt that it was our duty to see that no action which took place here should prevent the enterprise from being in position to deliver power on the first day of October last, and W'e took the steps which I have indicated.
Having done that and having seen "that the enterprise was in a position to deliver power, the further question arose as to what should be the attitude of the government. I endeavoured to make it perfectly clear that I could not recommend to this house the creation of a federal power commission to operate in a province a policy which was the exact negation of that of the government of that province. The policy of the government of Quebec is to regulate by appropriate authority the development of power by private enterprise. That is its considered policy and from that policy it has indicated that it has no intention of departing. To create a federal power commission which would take possession, by expropriation or other appropriate proceedings, of t!he property of a private enterprise, whether it be Beauharnois or any other company, was something that we did not care to contemplate and we therefore declined to consider that proposal. .
The company having defaulted in its bonds, the appropriate remedies provided by the trust deed under which $30,000,000 had been advanced became operative and a meeting of the holders of these securities was held. The government divested itself of any responsibility in connection with those investors as to how they should enforce the securities upon which they had made their advances. The}7 appointed a committee and that committee made a report, which was to the effect that a certain scheme of reorganization should be adopted. I was asked whether the position of the government would be the same if other plans were made with other enterprises or other individuals for the purpose of giving effect to the reorganization and I answered in the affirmative; the government had no interest as to individuals nor any communication directly or indirectly with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power. The committee of the bondholder's carried forward their negotiations and as a result of such negotiations the reorganization was arranged as proposed to the bondholders. Stone and Webster did see me and they asked that we should guarantee

Beauharnois-Mr. Bennett
securities, which I declined to do; and I declined to guarantee securities for the reorganizing committee. As a result of all the efforts that were made, a committee of the security holders put forward a plan at a meeting of all the $30,000,000 bondholders for the purpose of enabling them to say aye or nay to the proposals thus made, and the government left itself in a position where the same provisions that existed with respect to that plan would exist with respect to any plan that was put forward for the reorganization of the enterprise. The plan carried and the matter is ended so far as the government is concerned.
There is just one other observation which I desire to make. This house has listened to attacks against power monopoly in the province of Quebec. This house has no concern about what that province does within its constitutional limitations. It is, within the ambit of its jurisdiction, as complete and authoritative a legislative body as is this parliament within its own, and I decline to be drawn into any controversy as to the wisdom or uniwisdom of what Quebec may do within its legislative jurisdiction with respect to power or otherwise. I have endeavoured at all times, at least in my public life, to make clear that I regard the rights of provinces and provincial legislatures as being quite as important to maintain as are the rights and privileges of this parliament within their respective fields of legislative action. In this instance the province of Quebec, for reasons that may seem good to it but with respect to which I as a member of the Dominion parliament have no business to concern myself, has made the determination that it will proceed by private capital to develop its power resources and that it will create, as it has, a tribunal for the purpose of regulating and determining rates. All I can say is that any contest that may take place between the users of power and the corporation supplying it, for the purpose of securing a reduction in rates is a matter beyond the control of this parliament; it rests solely and entirely within the control and jurisdiction of the legislature of Quebec and the people who elect that legislature. As to the wisdom of their plans, I have nothing whatever to say.
That being so, there is only one further question that I think should be dealt with, and that is the export of power. With respect to the export of power from Canada to the United States, those who are interested will find that in 1925 the legislature of Quebec passed a statute, the preamble of which is as concise and powerful an indictment of any policy that will permit the export of power 53719-324J
as it is possible to conceive can be put into words. No stronger indictment as to the evil consequences that will flow from permitting the export of power to the United States can be found than will be found in that statute. But the province of Quebec has not the jurisdiction over the export of any commodity from this dominion. That rests within the jurisdiction of the dominion, and this parliament passed a statute which provides for licences being given before power or gas is exported from our country. There are outstanding certain export licences with respect to what is called surplus peak power, off peak power, if you will, at Niagara. I am not at the moment concerned about those, because they were granted many years ago and they have been continued even unto this day. But with respect to the granting of licences to export power, it is the considered judgment of this government as at present advised that we shall not grant any such licences. I say that for two reasons: first, that it has been the settled policy of this country to maintain that view; it has been the view of successive governments, although there was put forward here some years ago a proposal which was negatived largely through the efforts of my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). But the second view, which after all is the powerful and prevailing one in my judgment, is the one indicated a few days ago by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and expressed in terms, to which I need not again refer, by my colleague the leader of the Senate. Those words are as appropriate to-day as they were when they *were uttered. We cannot afford to export power and create community life in another country with industrial activities and then, when the requirements of our own country call for cutting off the licence for export, contemplate that situation without having regard to a statement made by a president of the United States that such action on our part would practically be considered an unfriendly act. Under those circumstances I make the statement I have made this morning for the purpose of relieving any doubt there may be in the minds of any hon. member that the government has in contemplation the granting of licences for the export of power. I shall not trouble the house further and I offer an apology for dealing at such length with this matter this morning, but I desire to summarize the position in a few Short sentences.
We came into this matter, the Beauharnois power development, in consequence of statements that were made in the house that
Beauharnois-Mr. Bennett

brought about an investigation by a committee selected by the House of Commons. That investigation resulted in certain recommendations being made to which this government gave effect. There was mentioned the other day one matter that I do not think was investigated by the committee and with respect to which it may be necessary for the government to make further inquiry; that is, the Jacques Cartier Investment Corporation or something of that sort, I am not just sure of the name, as regards which certain allegations were made in consequence of which we have made and will continue to make certain inquiries.
At the time there were outstanding contracts for about 400,000 horsepower with the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario and the Montreal Light, Heat and Power. There were restrictions upon the activities of t'he corporation in the selling and distribution of power. The corporation was a provincial one. The government gave it such assistance as was necessary to enable it to secure from the banks the funds required to start the enterprise, and within the time limit of the contracts, the enterprise began to function and supply power. Next, the government furnished every facility possible to enable those who had paid their $30,000,000 into the enterprise to meet together and determine what action they should take, whether by foreclosure that would vest all the shares of the company in them, or by reorganization. They determined upon a plan of reorganization which involved certain assistance being given in the way of extending the time within which to carry out their undertakings and sell their securities, which we made available to any company or persons who desired to participate in the enterprise.
Lastly, the government has incurred no further responsibility nor does it financially or otherwise in connection with this purely provincial matter, and we shall do everything in our power to see that the arrangements that have been made with the government are carried into effect, for in consequence of the contracts outstanding the government had no control over rates in any way, shape or form.
The observations which I made after the non. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) had spoken are veiy pertinent now, and they were then but for one fact, that I was not then aware that the enterprise had made its agreements which precluded any possibility of action being taken by this administration with respect to the price at which power was being sold or could be sold, or for that [Mr. Bennett. 1
matter, I suppose, taken by the late administration after the order in council had been passed.
I have nothing further to add except to say that every possible oportunity was afforded to those who owned the enterprise to do with it as they pleased, but that the government in pursuance of the policy adopted by this 'house practically unanimously afforded an equal opportunity to all who might be concerned to assert their rights and to deal with the situation amongst themselves as shareholders as they thought desirable.
As to my own view, I regretted and I still regret that it was possible for the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated to place itself in the position it did with respect to this enterprise, but that is a matter over which I had no control and over which this government has no control, but which arises by reason of the fact that the contract which was made with this Beauharnois enterprise by the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated is a contract that limited and limits I think for a period of seventy years-a lifetime contract-the right of the Beauharnois Corporation to distribute power practically within the whole island of Montreal. That we could not deal with because we had no power to destroy a contract validly made according to the laws of the province of Quebec between the two companies. Under those circumstances, with the full facts (before us, we took the only steps that could be taken to afford to those who had put their money in an opportunity for a breathing space in which to reorganize their enterprise and to take such steps as they thought desirable for the protection of their investment and the undertaking which has been built by reason of their investment being made.

The house resumed from Tuesday, May 16, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Duranleau for the second reading of Bill No. 106, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.

Mr. Speaker, in any remarks I have to make on the bill which is now before the house I intend to deal only with section 11, which relates to the coastal shipping of Canada. I think the minister frankly admitted last night that the bill was principally for the protection of ship owners, so we are justified in dealing with the bill from that standpoint. From a perusal of the evidence it is clear who is asking for this bill. It is the shipbuilders and the Shipping companies, and I think they are chiefly under one concern, Canada Steamships Limited. They are both shippers and shipbuilders. They own the Midland Shipbuilding Company of Midland and the Davie Shipbuilding Company of Levis. Prominent amongst the witnesses before the Senate committee I noticed the names of Mr. Enderby and Mr. Wolvin, Who figured so prominently in the association or combine that was responsible for raising grain rates on the great lakes in 1922, and which finally resulted in the appointment of a royal commission to investigate grain rates on the great lakes. As a result of that investigation two bills were introduced in the session of 1923, one placing these grain rates under the jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners, and the other giving the governor in council power to suspend the coastal shipping laws at any time.
I noticed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) last night, in the very able speech which he made on the second reading of this bill, said that it was the duty of parliament to promote the interests of the various industries in Canada, and he apparently was speaking of the shipowning industry. I think the ship-owning industry are very well able to take care of themselves, judging by their action of last year.

May I interrupt my hon.
friend? It is certainly not correct for him to state that I represent the ship owners. I do not represent anyone of that character or any business interest in this house.
Let me assure the minister I did not say he represented them at all.
You said that exactly.

No; Hansard will show I did not say that. I did not intend to say it, and if accidentally I did say it I shall quite gladly withdraw it. I said that his remarks last night were directed in defence of or in support of the interests of the ship owners.

No. Mr. Speaker, I must ask my hon. friend not to state it in that way, because it is not right. One can make an argument pro or con, but it does not necessarily follow that he represents the interests of any particular industries or particular class.

I shall gladly accept the statement of the minister and withdraw anything to which he may object. But I wish to make it plain that I think the ship owners are much better able to take care of their own interests than are the producers. I am very much concerned about the interests of the producers. I believe they are the ones who need protection. Mr. Enderby, when before the committee, was quite frank. He admitted the principal reason for the section of the bill to Which we are objecting is to give protection to Canadian shippers. The principal function of the Canadian fleet is the movement of the Canadian crop across the great lakes.

May I interrupt the hon.
member? Yesterday he asked me if there had been an order, I had not time to send it over then, I will do so now. There was an order actually passed by the board of grain commissioners on the 5th of May of this year. There is no necessity to wait for an investigation.

Mr. Speaker, the aim of this bill is to give to Canadian ships a monopoly of the carrying of Canadian grain on the great lakes. The minister himself put the situation last night in the statement that "Canadian boats should parry Canadian grain." The effect of this bill, if it becomes law, will be to deprive Canadian grain of the use of Buffalo as a transfer or a storage point. To understand the full effect of that on the transportation of grain, one must have in -mind the picture of the whole grain transportation business. When the first trainload of wheat leaves .the west for .the head of the lakes, those who ship it 
have no idea where it will ultimately land. When that wheat arrives at the terminals, those who own it do not know where it is going to go; it may be sold in any one of a dozen different countries. But one thing .they do know is that that wheat must be kept moving; they know there are millions and hundreds of millions of bushels to follow. They know if it is delayed in the terminals they will fill up, and if they do, the railway yards will be congested, the blockade will go right out to the farms and the wheat will not move. The whole strategy in .moving wheat consists in constantly moving it eastward, but always moving it to a point from which it may be shipped out in the greatest number of directions. That point is Buffalo. It is the .most strategically located point in Canada or the United States for the transfer and storage of grain. From that city you can ship down the St. iLawrence and out through Canadian ports or you can ship down the barge canal or by rail to New York, Boston, Portland or several other United States ports. You discover on a certain morning that you can sell some wheat in Liverpool, some in Bordeaux, Antwerp, Rotterdam or Hamburg. What do you do? The first thing is to see what ocean space you can get. You discover that coming into the port of Montreal is a ship that will load for Liverpool; coming into the port of Portland is a ship that will load, we will say, for Hamburg; coming into the port of Boston there is one that will load for Antwerp and coming into the port of New York is one that will load for Rotterdam and another that will load for Bordeaux. If you could not get your grain on to any ship loading for Antwerp or Amsterdam or Rotterdam or Hamburg or any other port, you would not be able to make the sale and the result would be that you would sell less grain. In the United States in 1880 the freight rate on wheat from Chicago to New York was 20 cents a bushel. Under free competition, open market conditions, that rate gradually worked down till at the turn of the century it was only 10 cents a bushel. Then it worked back and forth within a range of two cents a bushel until rate control became effective in the United States. Prior to 1906 their attempt to control rates had been spasmodic and ineffective. With the passing of the Hepburn Act in 1906, rate control became a reality, and then the decline in freight rates ceased. The rates moved back and forth within a range of two cents until 1916 when the rate shot up to 20 cents a bushel. day one of the reasons why Canadian boats cannot compete is that they have a lot of old-fashioned, out of date boats.

I have here a book on the American Transport System by Harold Moulton and associates in which this matter of freight rates is discussed, and he has this to say:
Wherever there is free economic competition it will decide the rate question, and it should be permitted to do so freely.

The legislation was drafted in fear of retaliation by the United States. I believe that it would 'have been brought in before but there was always the fear that the United States might hit back. At last some clever person, the government leader in the Senate I believe, 'hit upon the device of taking the very words out of the American act and putting them into the Canadian act, aiguing that surely the Americans cannot now retaliate against what we are doing, that they cannot resent these very words in our act which are taken from their own act. But the cases are not quite parallel. There is small temptation for Canadian boats to go into United States ports to carry grain to Canadian ports, and then go back to American
ports, because the ports are not favourably located. The cases are not parallel at all. It may have seemed very clever for the government leader in the Senate to devise this way of drafting the section so that the Americans would not retaliate. I say it may have been a clever trick of a clever man, but I have no faith in clever tricks of clever men as a basis of national prosperity. In trying to build the prosperity of a country you must take the broader and the longer view. Those tactics might be all right for a man running a pawn shop, but they will not do in international relations. The Americans will find a way to retaliate. What will they do to our boats on the Pacific coast running from Seattle to Vancouver and Skagway? Will they not find a way to retaliate? I think they will. To assume 'that simply by taking these words out of their act and putting them in ours we have outwitted them is not to give them credit for being as clever as we are, and I think we might be disappointed.
What about the tariff truce of which we have heard so much lately? A tariff truce has been arranged among the different countries. We are going to get together with the idea of promoting world trade. Is this proper preparation for it? I am not sure of the terms of the truce, and I do not know whether this legislation is a breach of it or not- certainly I do know it is a breach of the spirit of it. It is protection, pure and sr-uple. What about the talk of reciprocity? We are going to have a reciprocity treaty with the United States-perhaps. Is this good preparation for it? In what frame of mind wil the Americans be when they see this legislation on our books? What will they say when we seek more favourable trade relations? What about the seaway treaty? Will the United States enter into a seaway contract if we say we will not allow any American ships through our ports? They do not know what we may do next. Two years ago- nearly three years ago-our Prime Minister went abroad to do wonderful things for trade within the empire. He went to the Imperial conference at London. At that time he failed. A year ago he had another opportunity when the Imperial economic conference met here in Ottawa. We know the results of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Very tangible results.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Look at the trade returns.

Look at the pockets of the people.

Canada Shipping Act-Mr. Young

Now he has another opportunity. He is going to another conference to try to promote world trade. But before he goes he is making a similar preparation,-a preparation similar to that which he made before he went to the Imperial conference in London. Before he went to London he passed legislation which made the conference abortive. Before the conference at Ottawa last year legislation was placed upon our statute books which made it impossible to effect profitable trade arrangements with Great Britain. Now he is going to another conference, but before going he is introducing another measure which will have the effect of giving a monopoly of shipping on Canadian lakes to Canadians.
You want to create a monopoly for American ships.

No, I am asking only for free competition. That is all we ask. Let the grain be carried by whomsoever can carry it cheapest and most efficiently. There seems to be no limit to the ingenuity displayed by this government in devising ways and means of stifling Canadian trade.
Oh, oh.

And the strange part of it is that they do it all with the very best of intentions. They think that by this measure they are going to help us. They think they can build up Canadian shipping in this way. No country in the world has been able to build up its shipping industry by means of navigation acts or protective tariffs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Has the hon. member been reading what the British Shipping Federation has been saying lately about competition?
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If he had he would not now be making such observations about what he calls free competition.
I am making them, anyway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Everybody out of step
but my boy.

No country ever succeeded
in building up its shipping by navigation acts such as these. Norway tried it once. Centuries before Columbus discovered America the Scandinavians established colonies on this continent, with which they carried on a profitable shipping business. But what hap-

pened? They passed certain navigation acts which had in view the very purpose behind this bill, namely, to confine shipping to their own nationals. What were the results? They destroyed their colonies-destroyed them completely. England tried to build up her trade in the same way.
She did.

Let us see what she did.
In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries she passed her navigation laws. Here is the result.:
Sir Joseph Child in 1690 enumerated fifteen lines of foreign trade which we had lost either wholly or partly through the working of the navigation acts, while the Dutch broadly gained what we had lost.
Then on the next page:
But when we note at the same time that the tonnage of the mercantile marine, estimated on the annual clearances, had risen only from 444,000 in 1714, to 471,000 in 1760, we realize the utter failure of the navigation acts to fulfil their avowed purpose. In the same period the foreign tonnage entering English ports had^ increased more than fourfold, to say nothing of the smuggling mostly done in foreign bottoms.
In other words, the navigation acts, which England had passed for the sole purpose of protecting her shipping and giving to British ships a monopoly of the shipping trade, in forty-six years increased British shipping by three-quarters of one per cent, while foreign shipping into British ports increased by four hundred per cent. How much success did they have? How much success did their navigation laws reveal? I have much more that I could read, but I shall not take the time.
You might as well read it.
All right, I will.

Read some more, it is
really most pleasant reading.

I know it is pleasant for
my hon. friend.

And it happened only
about four or five hundred years ago.

The article is too long to
read, but the substance of it is this: France tried to build up her shipping in the same way, and failed; Venice tried it, and failed; Genoa tried it and failed; the United States tried it and failed. We are trying it and we are going to fail, because you cannot build up a shipping industry in that way. Shipping is the last industry in the world which will

Redistribution Bill
stand a protective tariff. It is the one industry above all other's which must have free, open competition. Something was said a few moments ago by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland)-

Will the hon. member
permit a question? He has just stated that this measure provides a protective tariff for shipping. There is no protection for shipping, in so far as the great British shipping world is concerned. They all have access to our waters, it is not limited to Canadian ships. The whole British shipping world, the largest entity in the whole shipping industry of the world, has access.
This, then, is levelled at the ships of one particular country? Is that right? Do I understand that?
No. All foreign shipping is included.'
All foreign shipping is included,-but it is aimed at the ships of one particular country.
No it is not.

It is. Last night the minister said that it is the business of parliament to nurture Canadian interests. To nurture them means to feed them. Where will he get the wherewithal to feed them? Is it the business of parliament to take from one man that which he produces and feed it to another? I say it is not. It is the business of parliament to see that every Canadian gets fair play. He is entitled to the thing and he should get the thing that he produces himself.
Hear, hear.

I cannot support this bill in any shape or form. If it is passed it will result in a monopoly of the trade on the great lakes. That trade will be delivered over into the hands of only Canadians. It will result in higher freight rates. It will result in difficulties in selling our wheat at a time when one of the greatest problems with which we are confronted is that of selling wheat. Because, as I said before, when the grain cannot be shipped from the most satisfactor}^ point, it very often happens that we miss the sale of a consignment. In every way we look at it this bill is unsatisfactory. I do not see how any hon. members from the west can support it. I see that the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) is in his seat. Will he stand up and vote for this bill; will he vote for a bill which will increase the freight rates on grain carried on the lakes?
53719-325	*

I will answer my hon. friend. Yes, I will vote for this bill. I think if the hon. member had heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night he must be satisfied that the grain growers in the west have every protection.
I heard what he said. It will be a very sony day for the hon. member when his people hear about his statement.
I have no worry at all.

What about the other members from the west? I do not see how they can vote for this bill. It is class legislation, and is designed to protect a certain class of people doing a certain business on the lakes, people who will be able to put their hands into the pockets of the western farmers, take money out of them and put it into their own pockets. Who is there who will guarantee him a price for his wheat? Nobody does and nobody can. Why then should he be compelled to guarantee profits to anyone else?

No one suggests it.
On motion of Mr. Kennedy (Peace River) the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house we may perhaps intervene in this debate for the purpose of reverting to the order of presenting reports of standing and select committees. It is quite unusual, and can only be done with the consent of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: What is the purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: For the purpose of receiving the report of the select committee dealing wth redistribution.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Before giving any consent on that point may I ask the Prime Minister what is the intention of the government with respect to the report, once it is brought in? Is it intended to go right on with the bill immediately?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
We could not go on until this order of business is disposed of. The purpose of dealing with it at the present moment is that the bill may be distributed. It was suggested after a conference yesterday, that we name two of the older members [DOT]-and I am suggesting that Sir George Perley and Mr. Duranleau should be the two from

Redistribution Bill

this side,-to confer with members who might be named by the leader of the opposition to see if such difficulties as exist in connection with the schedule to the bill can be disposed of. There are not a large number.
This house might then adjourn until three o'clock to-morrow, for the Minister of Marine is in charge of the bill now before the house, and if he continued with that he would not 'have the opportunity to confer. The Postmaster General, as is known, is attending a conference that, under an agreement, I think, was arranged to meet here, I fancy before we came into office. That has to be dealt with. Under these circumstances if the report is presented the consideration of it would go upon the order paper for the next sitting, the bill would be distributed and if it be acceptable to the house, we could adjourn until three o'clock to-morrow to enable this conference to take place.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Under the rules of the house it would not be possible to proceed with the bill in any event until it had been placed upon the order paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Not without consent.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
That woidd have to be given first. I would not feel that we were justified in giving consent until we have had an opportunity of at least looking over the schedules. In the circumstances it would appear to be desirable for the house to adjourn at one o'clock until to-morrow afternoon and in the interval have the conference to which the Prime Minister has referred.
The Prime Minister has mentioned the names of the gentlemen whom he would select. I would name Mr. Lapointe and Mr. Stewart (Edmonton) who are to my immediate right and left, to represent the official opposition. If that is agreeable, I would agree to the suggestion to revert to the order so as to permit the report to be introduced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Then by consent, I move, -I would associate with me the right hon. gentleman as seconder-that we revert to the order of presenting reports of standing and select committees.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: No, my right hon. friend has placed his faith in majorities, I think he had better hold thereto.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I would still be in a
majority. Seconded, then, by Mr. Stevens.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) presented the second and final report of the special committee as follows:
Your special committee to whom was referred Bill No. 2, an act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, with instructions to prepare schedules to contain and describe the several electoral divisions entitled to return members to this house and to report the same, now present their second and final report:-
Your committee have prepared the descriptions and the return of members for the several electoral divisions which are set forth in the schedules hereto appended in respect of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island and the Yukon territory.
The report of your committee is unanimous in so far as the same relates to Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Manitoba and the Yukon territory, and, although not unanimous as to the other provinces, represents a very substantial measure of agreement with respect thereto.
Accordingly the committee beg leave to report the said bill.
May I make a suggestion; I have not seen the bill-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It will be distributed immediately.

-but I would like to know the population of the new constituencies as determined and fixed by the bill. Would it be possible to have a list of those new constituencies with the population of each new riding described in the schedule so that we may be able to discuss the matter intelligently?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The bill is printed and
will be distributed now. The information the committee had before it will certainly be available to this select four who will try to deal with the problem. I should ask the chairman to make available all the information and maps that the committee had before it, which I believe indicate in approximate figures the population of the new ridings.
That is what I want.

If I may be permitted a word on this matter I also might instance that this is a rather unusual procedure. The proposal is that this house adjourn at one o'clock until three o'clock to-morrow in order that some of the older heads of this house, named by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, may confer together to iron out some of the difficulties that have arisen in the committee dealing with redistribution. It is rather unfortunate that this has

Redistribution Bill
to be done, but inasmuch as it has to be done, I think the suggestion is a very good one. But I think it is unfortunate that the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition should have agreed on the older heads of this house, because the longer a person remains in this house the more partisan he becomes, consequently the possibility of them accomplishing anything is not very great. The Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition have unfortunately forgotten that there is another section in this house that is as much interested in redistribution as the Conservative party and the Liberal party. If I may be bold enough to make a suggestion it would be that it would be advisable to have a younger head working with the older heads, and he would probably be the balance of power that would accomplish something. Therefore I suggest that we add to that committee Mr. Speakman of Red Deer to represent this corner of the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this informal discussion which by consent is being carried on may be all to the advantage of parliament. What we desire to do is to arrive at some fair redistribution of the seats in this dominion that will do violence to the rights of no man. That is the effort. Whether or not it can be accomplished depends largely upon the good will, as the right hon. gentleman opposite said yesterday, of those who comprise this house, having respect always to the fact that the anomalies of the past sometimes have to be undone. That does always create difficulty. Shifting population is always a factor. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) suggests that one member from that corner of the house might be of assistance on this committee. This small committee has no authority to bind anything. It will endeavour to speak for a party organization to ensure that the arrangements it makes may become effective; that is the position as I understand it. If the hon. member from Acadia, who has a fair mind, believes he can assist in the manner indicated, speaking for myself I shall be glad if he will sit in with the other members of the committee for the purpose of making any suggestions that might lead to that end. Would that be acceptable to my right hon. friend?

As far as the official opposition is concerned I would be most heartily in accord with having the leader of the Progressive party sit in with the other gentlemen for that purpose. The whole aim, as I understand it, is to arrive at what would 53719-325^
be recognized as fair and just as the result of persuasion and argument rather than of any other power or influence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so. Then it is understood that between now and to-morrow the small committee representing the parties, Sir George Perley; the Minister of Marine, Mr. Duranleau; the former Minister of Justice, the Hon. Mr. Lapointe; the former Minister of the Interior, the Hon. Mr. Stewart (Edmonton); and Mr. Gardiner, the hon. member for Acadia, shall meet together to see whether some suggestions can be made to obviate the necessity for prolonged and acrimonious discussion with respect to these matters.
Does the hon. member for Acadia feel equal to the task of representing the younger heads?
As my hon. friend will remember, I did not suggest that in the first place; I suggested the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We will take the leader of the party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I move, Mr. Speaker, that the house do now adjourn until to-morrow afternoon at three o'clock, but perhaps someone will move the adjournment of the debate first.

I move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker.
Motion agreed to and the debate adjourned.

Well, I object. There are many items on the order paper which might be taken up-items in which private members are interested.
The motion is not debatable. Does the hon. member desire to have a vote?
Yes.
